study.title: Leviticus 2 The offering of grains as a gift, sustenance and remembrance of the covenant
study.overview: Leviticus 2 regulates the grain offering, presented as a voluntary gift to the LORD. The chapter shows that the offer could take various forms - fine flour, baked, boiled or fried cakes, and toasted ears - but always with elements that highlighted consecration, purity and memory of the covenant: olive oil, incense and salt. Part of the offering was burned on the altar as "memorial," and the rest supported the priests. At the same time, the text forbids leaven and honey in what is burned to the LORD, and requires salt in every offering, ending with the offering of the firstfruits of the field.

outline.title: Fine flour, olive oil, incense and memorial portion
outline.explanation: The grain offering begins with fine flour on which olive oil and incense are placed. The priest burns only the representative portion, as a memorial, and the rest is to Aaron and his sons. This teaches that the whole offering belongs to God, although He also uses it to sustain his ministers.

outline.title: Various forms of preparation and the same consecration
outline.explanation: The text presents three preparation modes: in the oven, in the pot and in the frying pan. In all cases, the offer must be without leaven, and the memorial portion is burned on the altar. Diversity of forms does not change the principle: what is offered must be separated to God and treated as a most holy thing.

outline.title: Prohibitions and sign of the covenant
outline.explanation: Yeast and honey should not be burned to the LORD, while every offering must be seasoned with salt. The salt is called the salt of the covenant, indicating continuity, permanence and pactual fidelity. Here the sanctity of the offering is protected by clear limits and by a lasting sign of the relationship with God.

outline.title: Primitives of the field and final offer of the ears
outline.explanation: The final section deals with the firstfruits: toasted green ears and crushed grain, with olive oil and incense. Here too the priest burns the memorial portion. The principle remains the same: the first fruits of labor belong to the Lord and are presented with reverence.

study.context: The chapter is part of the Sacrifiole instructions given to Israel. The text presupposes the service of the descending priests of Aaron and the offering as an act of worship. The notes show that this offer could accompany other sacrifices, although here it also appears as an offer presented by itself, an expression of voluntary devotion. The agricultural backdrop is clear: flour, olive oil, ears and firstfruits belong to the daily lives of the people.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter highlights that God receives not only blood and animals, but also the fruit of human labor. The grain offering transforms daily food into worship, acknowledging that the provision comes from the Lord. The burning portion on the altar is called a memorial because it points to the memory of the covenant and for the total belonging of the offering to God. The prohibition of leaven can be understood, according to the commentators, as a rejection of all that corrupts or grows inappropriately; salt, in turn, symbolizes permanence and fidelity. The text also shows that holiness does not exclude the sustenance of priests: what is separated for God sustains his service. The firstfruits close the chapter reminding that the first part of the harvest belongs to the Lord before any personal use.

scholarViews.insight: The grain offering is presented as a gift to the Lord, an expression of worship that recognizes his sovereignty over the life of the worshiper.
The ban on leaven is applied as a warning against what spoils spiritual offerings; leaven becomes an image of pride, hypocrisy, wickedness, and corruption.
The salt represents duration and constancy; therefore it is called the salt of God's covenant, linked to the permanence of the covenant.

questions: What changes in our worship when we come to offer God not only words but also the concrete fruit of our work?
Is there any moral or spiritual "ferment" that is corrupting the sincerity of our offering to God?
How can we honor the principle of firstfruits by placing the Lord first in the use of what we receive?
study.practice: Intentionally separate the first part of your time, resources and work for God this week. Do this not as an empty ritual, but as a practical recognition that everything you possess comes from the Lord. Also examine your life to identify attitudes that need to be removed, so that your worship is pure, persevering and true.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided comment on the gift of cereals in general and bring some historical and symbolic details, but do not explain each verse in depth. Some interpretations, such as the precise meaning of leaven and honey, are presented as interpretive readings of the commentators, not as absolute definitions of the text. There is not enough base notes to state with certainty additional external details about location, date or exact practice at each stage of the ritual.
